title: The stunning transformation of the Southern Democratic Party, in one lifetime
paragraphs: Two of the biggest surprises of the 2026 election cycle were Democratic U.S. Senate victories in the Deep South. In addition to Annie Andrews’ victory in South Carolina, Scott Colom won a close contest in Mississippi, a place that historian James Cobb called “The Most Southern Place on Earth.”

Colom is not Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator. Two Black Republicans represented the state during Reconstruction, when state legislatures still selected U.S. senators. But Colom is the state’s first popularly elected Black U.S. senator. He is also the first Democrat that Mississippians have sent to the Senate since 1982.

It is tempting to read this change using a familiar political science term: party realignment. But as political scientists who study political campaigns and Southern politics, we see an equally important transformation in the electorate – the people who can cast votes.

Simply put, the Democratic Party in the South was transformed from a party that defended white supremacy and Black disenfranchisement into one in which Black voters became a central constituency. The Democrats who held Mississippi’s Senate seats for the majority of the 20th century were chosen by an electorate built to exclude Black citizens. Colom was elected by a dramatically different electorate and represents a very different Democratic Party.
To understand the magnitude of the change in Mississippi, it helps to look at the Democrats who came before Colom, what they stood for, and the political power they wielded.

For a brief period after the Civil War, Black Mississippians exercised real political power. They were a majority of the state’s population and, with the right to vote, helped elect the state Legislature that sent Hiram Revels to the U.S. Senate in 1870 and Blanche Bruce in 1875, both of them Black.

That period did not last. White Democrats regained control of Mississippi government in the 1870s, aided by political violence, intimidation and electoral fraud. In 1890, the state adopted a new constitution that used poll taxes, literacy tests and other restrictions to systematically disfranchise Black voters. Two years after the new constitution took effect, the percentage of Black men registered to vote had fallen to just 5.4 percent.

The result fundamentally changed Mississippi politics. For the next several generations, the Democratic Party dominated a political system in which most Black Mississippians had little meaningful voice. Republican electoral victories were rare. One newspaper in 1963 claimed that the election of Lewis McAllister to the state House was the party’s first win in 43 years. Without a competitive general election, winning the Democratic primary often meant winning office, and the politicians who emerged from a one-party system made possible by Black disenfranchisement became some of the most powerful political figures in the state’s history.

What happened in Mississippi reflected a broader pattern across the South. In 1949, political scientist V.O. Key published his seminal study of the region, “Southern Politics in State and Nation.” Key argued that the solid Democratic South rested on systematic disenfranchisement of Black voters.

The one-party system helped keep Black Southerners out of political power while allowing white Southern politicians to present a unified front against efforts to dismantle segregation and expand Black voting rights, particularly when those efforts came from the federal government. Mississippi was among the clearest examples of that system.

Before Colom, the last Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi was John Stennis in 1982. He first won election in 1947, filling the seat of Theodore Bilbo, who had won reelection in 1946 after a campaign in which he urged white Mississippians to keep Black voters away from the polls. Stennis won a 1947 special election with 52,068 votes in a state of 2.2 million people. He held that seat for 41 years.

Throughout much of his career, Stennis was an ardent segregationist. In 1956, he was one of 101 members of Congress from the South who signed what was called the “Southern Manifesto.” In that statement, these lawmakers denounced the Supreme Court’s decision in Brown v. Board of Education, in which the justices ruled that the “separate but equal” standards of racial segregation were unconstitutional; Stennis and the other signatories pledged resistance to school desegregation.
Later in his Senate career, Stennis was the only Southern Democrat who voted to oppose the creation of a national holiday honoring Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr.

Stennis’ Senate colleague for much of his tenure, Mississippi Democrat James Eastland, was an equally staunch defender of segregation. A cotton planter from the Mississippi Delta, he was appointed to the Senate in 1941 and won the seat outright in 1942. He remained in the Senate until 1978.

The day after the Supreme Court handed down its 1954 decision in Brown v. Board of Education, Eastland was quoted saying, “the South will not abide by nor obey this legislative decision by a political court.”

Recent attention has understandably focused on Stennis, the last Democrat to represent Mississippi in the Senate. When Colom takes office, he will occupy the Senate seat once held by Eastland and Democrat James Vardaman, who said that “if it is necessary every Negro in the state will be lynched; it will be done to maintain white supremacy.”

One-party rule also gave Mississippi’s senators unusual power. With little electoral competition, they could remain in office for decades. In a Senate where seniority mattered, longevity translated into influence.

Eastland, for example, chaired the Senate Judiciary Committee for more than two decades, giving him enormous influence over civil rights legislation. During his chairmanship of the powerful committee, that committee became known as “the graveyard of civil rights legislation,” according to the Senate’s website.

The Voting Rights Act of 1965 helped dismantle the electoral system that had sustained these men in office. Before it, fewer than 10% of Black Mississippians were even registered to vote. Within a few short years, a majority were.

Black voters increasingly aligned with the Democratic Party as its national leaders embraced civil rights, even while many Democratic officeholders in Mississippi continued to defend segregation. That meant Black voters sometimes supported incumbent white segregationists. The party’s voters changed faster than many of its candidates did.

The 1978 election for the seat Colom will hold illustrates how complicated that transition could be. After Eastland retired, Charles Evers, brother of slain civil rights leader Medgar Evers, ran as an independent and drew nearly a quarter of the vote. His candidacy split the traditionally Democratic vote, helping Republican Thad Cochran win with a mere plurality.
By the 21st century, white Mississippians overwhelmingly supported Republican candidates, and Republican dominance had replaced the old Democratic dominance in most statewide elections.
That pattern made Colom’s victory all the more striking. He won with overwhelming support from Black voters while also attracting enough white voters to build a winning statewide coalition.

The contrast with Mississippi’s old Democratic coalition could hardly be sharper. The Democratic Party of Vardaman, Bilbo, Eastland and Stennis maintained its power in part by keeping Black Mississippians away from the ballot box with violence and Jim Crow laws.

title: How the US power rivalry with Russia and China is turning outer space into the next battlefront
paragraphs: U.S. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink recently confirmed that the United States has weapons deployed in Earth’s orbit. To date, the U.S. Space Force, the space service branch of the U.S. armed forces, has provided relatively few details about what these weapons are or what they can do except that they are what Meink called “on-orbit space control weapons.”

Meink’s announcement is significant, but not necessarily because the U.S. is the first country to place weapons in orbit. For years, the U.S., Russia and China have accused each other of developing and testing such capabilities, although none has publicly acknowledged deploying space weapons – until now.

We are scholars of space law and governance, and our research illustrates the challenges of uniting diverse groups to establish norms related to the use of resources, safety zones and conflict prevention in new domains such as space. Without better communication and deeper coordination between the world’s space powers, we could witness the beginning of a space arms race.
In 1981, the United Nations added the Prevention of an Arms Race in Outer Space, known as PAROS, to its agenda.
More than four decades of diplomatic efforts under PAROS have produced meager results, though there was a United Nations agreement in 2024 that made progress on reducing threats.

Despite many countries’ proclamations supporting space arms control, no multilateral treaty banning weapons in space has been adopted. With global arms control generally in retreat, and the apparent lack of political will among the three major space powers, efforts to control space weapons have reached an impasse.
The question increasingly is not whether an arms race in space can be prevented, but how it will be managed.
The Outer Space Treaty of 1967, to which all major space powers are parties, is often described by scholars, practitioners and policymakers as the constitution of outer space.

Article IV of the treaty remains the only legally binding international provision specifically regulating weapons in outer space. The article prohibits countries from placing nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction in orbit around Earth. It also imposes a broader prohibition on military activities on the Moon and other celestial bodies, including establishing military bases, testing weapons and conducting military maneuvers.

However, the article does not prohibit conventional weapons in Earth’s orbit. That omission is significant. The treaty can be understood as implicitly permitting what it does not prohibit: the placement of such weapons in orbit.

China has used these ambiguities as cover for its own space weaponization efforts. In a 2007 test, China destroyed one of its own satellites while in orbit, and it has recently deployed a mysterious space plane.

China, nonetheless, reacted critically to the recent U.S. weapons announcement. In September 2026, it urged Washington to stop expanding its military presence in space. That same month, Russia renewed calls for the demilitarization of outer space.

Both countries have long advocated stronger international restrictions on space weapons. Russia and China twice jointly proposed a treaty prohibiting the placement of weapons in outer space. The U.S. opposed the proposals in 2014, pointing to their failure to also cover important ground-based, anti-satellite weapons.
But Russian and Chinese declarations in favor of keeping weapons out of space sit uneasily alongside their own activities.

In 2020, U.S. Space Command, part of the Defense Department, accused Russia of testing a space-based anti-satellite weapon after an orbiting Russian satellite released a projectile. Russia said the spacecraft was performing an inspection mission.
In 2024, the United States said Russia had launched another satellite, Cosmos 2576, which it assessed to be a “counter space” weapon capable of attacking other satellites.

China has similarly demonstrated increasingly sophisticated operations in orbit. Five Chinese spacecraft conducted satellite flybys in 2024, an exercise that a senior U.S. Space Force officer later described as practicing “dogfighting in space.”

None of this proves that every suspicious Russian or Chinese spacecraft is a weapon. Many technologies used for servicing, inspection and maneuvering around satellites are inherently dual-use. But it does put Moscow’s and Beijing’s calls to keep weapons out of space in perspective.

It also illustrates the security threat now taking shape. Washington can point to Russian and Chinese activities to justify its own weapons. Moscow and Beijing can now point to acknowledged U.S. weapons to help justify their actions, which could result in a self-fulfilling prophecy.

Space has been part of warfare for decades. The 1991 Gulf War has sometimes been called the first “space war” because of the unprecedented role satellites played in navigation, communications, intelligence and targeting. But satellites primarily supported military operations taking place on the ground.
That distinction has gradually eroded. NATO formally recognized space as a military theater in 2019.
Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine then demonstrated something different, in which the very definition of a weapon was challenged.

Hours before Russian troops crossed the border, a cyberattack disrupted the U.S. satellite network Viasat, in what was dubbed by commentators as the first “space-cyber war.” Space-based services were no longer merely supporting military operations but were themselves deliberately targeted as part of a military campaign.

The acknowledgment of weapons in orbit represents another step in that evolution. Space assets are transitioning from systems that primarily support warfare in other domains to systems that can be weapons, targets and participants in combat and are often replete with vulnerabilities that could be exploited by an adversary.

title: Today’s Thanksgiving holiday was invented amid the Civil War to unite a divided country
paragraphs: It is hard to imagine a more American holiday than Thanksgiving. Every year, elementary schoolers learn about the first celebration: that after surviving a terrible year, New England’s first European immigrants, the Pilgrims, invited their Indigenous neighbors to a feast in gratitude for their help and God’s providence.

Children learn the story as if it were history – and as though Americans have commemorated Thanksgiving the same way ever since. The only existing eyewitness account of this event does not, however, say much about what was eaten. A slightly later account of the 1621 harvest mentions seasonal food such as venison, corn – and, yes, turkeys.

The idea of a straight line connecting that “first Thanksgiving” to Thanksgivings today is, in fact, an American myth. It is a story created in the 19th century to unify a nation and long used to assimilate new immigrants into it.

The Pilgrims and Puritans, who started arriving in Massachusetts shortly afterward, regularly held fasts and feasts. On fast days, the community atoned for sins they believed they had committed. On feast days, they gave thanks to God. Some governors of colonies – and later, states – declared fall holidays of thanksgiving, but did not coordinate with each other.

The Thanksgiving that we know, with the traditional recipes and the close connection to the Pilgrims, was largely the creation of one woman: Sarah Josepha Hale, who was born in New Hampshire in 1788. In the 1830s she became the editor of Godey’s Lady’s’ Book, which had the largest circulation of any U.S. magazine before the Civil War.

Godey’s included clothing patterns, recipes, articles on home management, essays on educating children, recipes and fiction. Hale believed that the woman was the heart of the home and responsible for creating an upstanding, God-fearing, wholesome family.

She was also deeply committed to her young country and believed that homemakers could help create its national identity. According to historian Elizabeth Pleck, Hale began publishing editorials calling for a national Thanksgiving, along with instructions for what the day could look like.

Godey’s taught readers how to celebrate the day, with recipes for seasonal food such as turkey and cranberry sauce. The centerpiece of the table was the pies, which featured elaborate pastry decorations: the Mayflower or a cornucopia, created out of pie crust. The full table was a celebration of “women’s work,” at a time when the Industrial Revolution was shifting the economy toward factories and other business, making the importance of unpaid domestic labor less obvious.

Hale’s idea of Thanksgiving also emphasized returning to loved ones, as those factories were drawing many workers away from home. She saw it as a day to tell family stories – and the story of the nation, starting with the first Thanksgiving.

Hale petitioned five presidents to declare Thanksgiving a national holiday. Abraham Lincoln finally took her up on it, hoping that a national holiday emphasizing the country’s origin story would prove uniting during the Civil War.

Northern women sent pies to the families of soldiers and turkeys to the men at the front. Pleck notes that abolitionist Sojourner Truth went door to door, collecting funds to provide Thanksgiving dinners to African American troops.

The holiday caught on gradually. Given the Protestant origins of early Americans’ feast and fast days, Catholics were slow to embrace it. Given its association with Lincoln and the war, the South was also late to adopt it. And given the day’s emphasis on family, it was less celebrated on the frontier, where single men dominated.

Wherever Thanksgiving was celebrated, however, Godey’s Lady’s Book taught Americans how to celebrate it. The magazine’s op-eds connected the holiday menu and the past, using the Pilgrims’ courage to inspire 19th-century Americans dealing with massive changes in their own lives: war, industrialization, urbanization and the frontier.
Before long, Thanksgiving was also seen as a way to assimilate immigrants.

This vision was, in part, popularized by political cartoonist Thomas Nast. “Uncle Sam’s Thanksgiving Dinner,” which appeared in Harper’s Weekly in 1869, depicted Americans from any number of races and ethnicities in their national dress: men, women and children sitting as equals around a dinner table, with portraits of presidents on the wall, while Uncle Sam carved a turkey.

The image suggested that immigrants could be incorporated into the nation – and formerly enslaved people, too. It was printed just one year after the 14th Amendment granted citizenship to anyone born in the U.S. and four years after the 13th Amendment formally ended slavery.

Nast’s image contrasted sharply to another cartoon, also called “Uncle Sam’s Thanksgiving Dinner,” that G.F. Keller drew for the San Francisco Wasp eight years later. Keller’s disheveled and entirely male collection of diners each ate their own national food, or offensive stereotypes thereof, suggesting immigrants could never truly become American.

But many Americans believed they could – although they demanded most immigrants give up their “Old World ways” and take on customs of their new country. Thanksgiving was part of the engine of that assimilation.

In the early 20th century, public schools taught about Thanksgiving and sent children home with recipe cards so that their parents could cook the same kinds of recipes Hale had popularized in the previous century. Schools framed the Pilgrims and their first Thanksgiving as the spiritual, if not literal, ancestors of all Americans: the first “immigrants.” They didn’t dwell on how the Pilgrims’ arrival looked more like colonization than immigration.

The holiday became a way to include newcomers in the national myth. By the 1920s, in fact, Thanksgiving was the most celebrated holiday in public schools. Pleck quotes one Jewish immigrant reflecting on his childhood and saying the Pilgrims were a way to connect “us offspring of Jewish immigrants – our own exiled fathers who had crossed the seas – and the traditions of Protestant America.” Students acted out the first Thanksgiving and were told they belonged to a “nation of immigrants.”

While some immigrant parents rejected the holiday, others embraced it, with spins to make it their own. Many served a turkey surrounded by the celebratory dishes of their own cultures. For Jews, the early 1900s invention of Crisco as a nondairy butter substitute allowed them to create a truly “American” Thanksgiving and dessert, without violating kosher rules against mixing meat and milk.

The fact that most families celebrate at home allowed immigrants and their children to take part in the national culture, while still expressing their own. During my own New England childhood, an Indian neighbor had my mother’s fairly classic cranberry relish, and by the end of the weekend she’d worked out a cranberry chutney with Indian spices. When we had Thankgiving dinner with my parents’ friends the Stalzmans, who were Jewish, matzah ball soup was the opening course.

At times, the idea of the Pilgrims arriving on the Mayflower has been used to exclude – to imply that only Americans whose literal ancestors came over on the ship, and other white Protestants like them, truly belong. Yet on the holiday in their memory, generations of new Americans affirmed that they, too, belonged.

title: ‘Strict liability’: The legal standard that could help rein in AI
paragraphs: Some people have begun using the legal system to rein in AI companies and the harms they are creating. Cases are mounting.

In October 2026, the parents of Bowen Wan sued OpenAI, charging that it’s ChatGPT agent may have instructed their daughter to stop taking her medication, leading to her death. In 2024, a mother sued the Character.AI company, claiming that its chatbot’s interactions with her son contributed to his suicide. The state of Kentucky later filed suit, claiming that Character.AI’s software exposed minors to self-harm and psychological manipulation.
Social media companies, powered by artificial intelligence, are also facing lawsuits about injuries they purportedly caused.
Regulating AI was a hot issue during the 2026 midterms, too. Several candidates who won their races have a regulation agenda.
I am a former litigator and a professor of business law, and all this action signals to me that people are looking to the law to protect them from AI harm.

But what is the legal liability of AI software? An answer may be found in a principle known as strict liability. Applied properly, strict liability could restrain the risky parts of the AI industry and still allow it to provide the tools the public wants.

Tort law protects people from negligence, such as who is responsible if you slip and fall in a store. Strict liability is part of tort law, but it is used to hold a person or company responsible for harm even if they were not at fault, not negligent or had no intent of creating trouble.

Two types of strict liability matter for AI. One addresses abnormally dangerous activity, such as blasting with dynamite or transporting radioactive material. The other addresses when a product hurts someone using it.

AI programs likely fit the abnormally dangerous standard. The touchstone case was tried in the U.K. in 1868. In the decision, the court stated that if someone has “anything” under their power that is “likely to do mischief if it escapes, [he] must keep it in at his peril” and is “answerable for all the damage which is the natural consequence of its escape.” The defendant is liable even if they used “the utmost care to prevent the harm.”

An attorney could pursue this avenue if a company builds AI software that is supposed to stay in a sandbox – a place isolated from the rest of a computer or network – but loses control of it. The AI industry’s recent admissions that the software creates all sorts of risks would make such cases stronger. When Anthropic filed for its initial public offering in October, numerous pages of the document detailed extraordinary risks that its frontier AI models could pose.

One hitch in applying this type of strict liability is that an activity must not be in common usage. Lawyers could make a strong case against so-called rogue AI that runs wild and isn’t available to most people.

Applying the danger standard could still fail to rein in AI companies or reward victims appropriately. In 1929, aviation was seen as abnormally dangerous. But damages were capped at US$8,300, which was not a large deterrent.

Attitudes changed in 1999, when the Montreal Convention standardized strict liability rules for international flights worldwide. It raised statutory damages and eliminated caps for negligence claims. Perhaps the most powerful tool in aviation liability today is for an authority to ground a company’s aircraft, which happened to Boeing after two fatal crashes with its 737 MAX planes.

Strict product liability is the other strategy for holding AI companies responsible for harm. In years past, courts tended to not see software as a product because it is intangible. But that view is shifting. In recent lawsuits alleging that social media hurt people, courts did see social media as a product and concluded that strict liability was applicable. Cases against Facebook have fallen into this category.

Character.AI’s recent bankruptcy filing came in part because of a lawsuit in which the court treated the software as a product. “Design defects” is the part of the doctrine gaining traction. To use this, a plaintiff shows that the product posed a foreseeable risk to someone using it. So far, the doctrine has worked when applied to the lack of guardrails in chatbots.

Pursuing strict liability could still run into snags. A court might order that AI software be turned off, or “grounded,” until it is improved. But as AI software creeps closer to being an operating system and is evermore embedded in everyone’s daily activities, it becomes difficult to suspend its use.

AI software by its nature is constantly “learning” and therefore changing. It is impossible for a company to promise that AI software will absolutely behave a certain way. In many cases, AI software is inherently incapable of supporting a guarantee about design safety. Still, strict liability is a way to hold the maker responsible, “even when those products evolve in ways not specifically desired or foreseeable by their manufacturers,” according to a Brookings Institution report.

I believe that if people are going to accept AI software as a boon to society, tough rules and sharp deterrents are needed. A strict liability system would shift risk from society to the companies seeking vast revenues.

The next steps will be sorting out whether to treat all or some AI software as a product, and whether the technology is ultrahazardous. If it is treated as that dangerous, AI can develop with incentives to reduce harms and ensure that people injured are compensated.
Deven Desai owns shares in Google, Inc. He received unrestricted research gifts from Google, Inc. and Facebook, Inc. a decade ago. He has not been employed by Google since 2010.

title: Your gut bacteria helps your body keep track of time, and when you eat influences how much nutrition you get from food
paragraphs: How your body processes food is significantly influenced by daily rhythms tied to 24-hour light-dark cycles. In new research published in the scientific journal Cell Host & Microbe, my colleagues and I found that the microbes living in your gut are the hidden timekeepers behind this system.

Gut microbes convert dietary signals into molecules that intestinal cells use to synchronize nutrient absorption with feeding times. In mice, this microbe-controlled timing mechanism maximizes the nutrients the mouse’s body takes in and supports growth, especially when food is scarce.
When mice consumed an excess of calories, however, that same system fueled obesity.

Because of Earth’s rotation, all animals – including humans – experience rhythmic shifts of day and night. Your eyes and brain use light signals to coordinate your body’s activities with environmental changes and nutrient availability. Disruption of this temporal alignment, such as through jet lag and night-shift work, is associated with a range of health disorders.

However, light is not the only timekeeper. Your intestines are home to trillions of microbes, called the gut microbiome. They play a key role in shaping your physiology, such as metabolism, immunity and even brain activity.

Intriguingly, the microbiome also influences the daily biological rhythms of hosts. My colleagues and I had previously shown that depleting gut bacteria in mice weakens circadian rhythms in the small intestine and alters them in the colon. These disruptions can affect how well your intestine absorbs and processes fats and other lipids, which may contribute to metabolic disorders such as obesity.
But if gut microbes are never exposed to the light, how do they track time? New research from my team suggests that the answer is feeding time.

We found that the gut microbiota can metabolize phytate – a food component commonly found in grains, beans, nuts and seeds – and convert it into molecules that activate a specific protein in intestinal cells, subsequently turning on genes involved in transporting nutrients. Conversely, when fasting, a decrease in phytate levels leads to reduced microbial activity and a drop in nutrient absorption.
Through this pathway, microbes align intestinal absorption with when you typically eat, which maximizes the efficiency of nutrient absorption.
Our findings suggest that, like light, food provides time-of-day signals that gut microbes read to determine how your body functions.
People have co-evolved with their gut microbiota for millennia, implying this microbe-controlled time system carries benefits.

For most of human history, food was scarce. We hypothesized that this microbial pathway might help people survive and grow under starvation conditions. To test this idea, we fed mice a nutrient-poor diet and gave some of them either a common gut microbe or a molecule it produces that is linked to circadian regulation. We found that undernourished young mice who were given this bacterium or the microbial molecule grew taller and healthier than mice that weren’t, suggesting that this microbial pathway promotes growth and metabolic health when nutrients are limited.

However, many people today have constant access to abundant calories. Rather than nutrient scarcity, obesity has become the dominant dietary challenge. We found that for mice under high-calorie conditions, this microbial pathway promotes excess fat uptake in the body and worsens diet-induced obesity.
Therefore, the same gut microbiome mechanism that helped people thrive can become a liability when it encounters an environment it was never designed for. This is an example of evolutionary mismatch.

title: Why Americans are losing confidence in public education
paragraphs: Americans’ satisfaction with public education has fallen to its lowest level since 1999.
Less than a third of Americans were satisfied with public education in 2026, compared with more than half who felt this way in 2019 and 1999, according to a September 2026 Gallup poll.

Parents typically give their own children’s education higher marks, reflecting a broader tendency to view familiar local institutions more favorably. But parents’ satisfaction with their children’s schools has also reached a record low: 66% of parents reported being satisfied in 2026, down from 83% in 1999.

Declining test scores, misinformation about public education, culture war issues and a general lack of knowledge about what K-12 schools are teaching have all contributed to this drop in satisfaction.

As an education researcher focused on family, school and community relationships, I am concerned that declining satisfaction in public schools could have lasting consequences for students and communities.
Public education in the U.S. was shaped by 19th-century advocates who argued that universal, free and nonsectarian education was essential to the success of a democratic society.

Communities agreed to invest in education because they believed it would benefit everyone, not just families with children, by supporting economic growth and preparing people to work together to solve shared problems.
Sustaining that public investment depends in part on people’s confidence that schools are delivering on these shared goals.

Without that public confidence, schools may struggle to secure the necessary funding and buy-in from the community. Parents may start to doubt that their children will be well-educated in public schools.
The rise of political polarization in the U.S. has complicated people’s perceptions of education.

Local schools have become flash points in debates over race, gender and what children should learn, and research on school board meetings shows how these conflicts can fuel distrust of school leaders and disrupt how schools are run.

For example, some conservative politicians, media outlets and advocacy groups have promoted false claims that schools are using critical race theory – meaning the idea that racism is built into laws, rules and everyday systems in society – to indoctrinate children.

Researchers found that these campaigns have often distorted lessons about racism and efforts to support students from diverse backgrounds, despite no evidence that critical race theory was widely taught in K-12 schools.
Repeatedly hearing and reading misinformation about public education can make it harder for communities to distinguish reliable, fact-based information from politicized distortions of reality.
The effects of misinformation can also extend into other areas of school life, including the work that district superintendents and school boards do.

In a 2026 study, my colleagues and I found that 82% of district superintendents felt increasingly concerned about inaccurate information circulating about their schools or district decisions. Another 55% reported that school board meetings had become noticeably more contentious over the past few years.
Such conflicts can become expensive.

Disputes over teaching about race and racism, the rights of LGBTQ+ students and access to books cost public schools US$3.2 billion during the 2023-24 school year. This estimate includes legal expenses, security, staff time and the cost of replacing employees who left because of tension or fighting at schools.
Controversy and polarization surrounding public schools can leave teachers feeling that their work is not trusted or valued.
Approximately 47% of teachers believed most Americans trusted teachers little or not at all, according to a 2023 Pew Research Center survey.
Teachers who feel valued are more likely to want to stay in the profession. Feeling undervalued may make an already demanding profession less appealing.
Regaining people’s trust in public education would involve the difficult task of addressing legitimate public concerns, like students’ declining test scores.
It would also involve effectively correcting misinformation and diplomatically managing community members’ diverse values and opinions.
Transparency is not just about giving community members more access to information about what schools are teaching and how.

title: Lucía Caminos is the first Latina ‘Grand Theft Auto’ lead – these video game characters paved the way
paragraphs: If the Netflix-exclusive trailer that briefly crashed the streaming service in August 2026 is any indication, “Grand Theft Auto VI” – a Bonnie-and-Clyde-style crime saga set in a satirical, fictionalized Florida – may be the most anticipated video game of all time.

It’s been 13 years since gaming company Rockstar released a new title in its flagship franchise. Fans have spent years dissecting leaked footage, constructing elaborate theories about the game’s mechanics and even attempting to reconstruct its fictional map using real-world geography.

But as a Latino studies scholar who teaches and researches video games, I’m most excited by the fact that “Grand Theft Auto VI” is the first title in the series to feature a Latina lead character: Lucía Caminos.
Not everyone is thrilled about a female protagonist – sexism, after all, remains a persistent issue in the gaming community.

But it nonetheless represents a watershed moment, as Latina video game characters have historically played second fiddle. Latino popular culture scholar Frederick Luis Aldama has pointed out how Latinos usually exist as obstacles for players to overcome rather than heroes whose stories players get to experience firsthand.

At the same time, a host of Latina characters throughout video game history – some playable, most not – paved the way for Lucía. Together, they show how representation is less about skin color and more about connection, complexity and character development.
In 1985, Carmen Sandiego was introduced as a criminal mastermind in “Where in the World is Carmen Sandiego?”
Players must pursue Carmen as she leaves a trail of clues across the globe. But Brøderbund, the game’s developer, left Carmen’s ethnic identity and origins ambiguous.

While researching the Brøderbund Collection at the Strong Museum of Play, I learned that the game’s creators originally imagined Carmen as a man named Estaban Devious who was born in Andorra, a tiny country in the Pyrenees with a large Spanish-speaking population. Brøderbund eventually settled on Carmen Sandiego – a name deemed exotic and befitting of a world traveler.

Despite Carmen’s unclear origins, Latinas have long connected with her. Actress Gina Rodriguez was so taken with Carmen as a kid that she jumped at the chance to voice Carmen in the animated series “Carmen Sandiego,” which premiered on Netflix in 2019 and ran for four seasons. According to Rodriguez, Carmen was “an incredible, strong, feminist, badass Latina who was going around the world. … I wanted to be just like her.” This cartoon gave Carmen a clear backstory – she was Argentine – and complicated her portrayal as a villain by having her turn on the very criminal organization she once belonged to.

With the show introducing Carmen Sandiego to a new generation of kids, new titles continue to appear. To coincide with Carmen’s 40th anniversary, “Carmen Sandiego” was released in 2025. It finally makes Carmen a playable character.
Like Carmen Sandiego, Isabela Keyes is a villain. One of the antagonists of the 2006 game “Dead Rising,” Isabela is the sister of Carlito Keyes, who initiates a zombie outbreak in Colorado.

Players discover that Isabela and Carlito infected people with the zombie virus to avenge the destruction of their hometown, Santa Cabeza, a fictional Central American village. The U.S. government had been experimenting with the virus there and destroyed the town to cover up its research.
But Isabela eventually realizes that she and Carlito have gone too far. She has a change of heart and ends up turning against her brother.

I think of Isabela as an important Latina video game character because she’s not simply included as a pretty face. That’s too often been the case for Latina characters, whether it’s Cynthia Velasquez in “Silent Hill 4” – whose alternate costume in the game made her look like a Playboy bunny – or Katarina Alves in “Tekken 7,” whose default and alternate costumes prominently feature her thong.

Capcom, the studio that produced the game, nonetheless marketed Isabela as a sex symbol. The question of how to interpret this sort of sexualization has divided gamers and scholars. On the one hand, many game designers still see their target audience as heterosexual men. However, women now make up half the gaming market, and overtly sexualized characters, which continue to appear, could further the sexism that bedevils the industry.
Video games have historically featured few queer characters, let alone queer Latino characters.

But indie games, which are developed outside major studios and often prioritize creative experimentation over commercial conventions, have generally been more welcoming to LGBTQ+ narratives and representation.

Fullbright’s 2013 exploration game “Gone Home” tells a 1990s coming-out story. Players explore the empty Oregon home of Katie Greenbriar and gradually learn the story of her younger sister, Sam, and Sam’s Mexican American girlfriend, Lonnie DeSoto, who hopes to one day join the military.

Though Lonnie is not a playable character, players piece together her experiences through letters and other clues. They learn about the challenges Lonnie faces as a Latina lesbian in the Junior Reserve Officers Training Corps, a high school program that teaches military-style leadership and discipline. By incorporating aspects of 1990s zine culture, the U.S. military’s Don’t Ask, Don’t Tell policy toward homosexuality and the feminist punk movement Riot Grrrl, “Gone Home” accurately and realistically captured the hopes and fears of being LGBTQ+ in the 1990s.

For years, playable Latina characters were pretty much nonexistent. Opportunities almost exclusively came from the large rosters of fighting games – characters like Ángel in the 2001 game “King of Fighters” and Christie Monteiro in “Tekken,” also released in 2001.
Over the past decade, that’s started to change.

Sombra is a Mexican hacker and one of the most prominent characters in the 2016 futuristic shooter “Overwatch.” Born Olivia Colomar, she was orphaned as a child and grew up in Mexico, where she developed extraordinary computer skills. She works with the game’s antagonists but pursues her own agenda of unraveling a global conspiracy.

Zyanya Mondragón, better known as Reyna, is a Mexican character in the 2020 futuristic shooter “VALORANT.” Reyna is a supernatural warrior who absorbs the life energy of enemies she kills, using it to heal herself and grow stronger. But her bloodthirsty nature has a deeply personal motivation: She needs the life energy she harvests to keep her younger sister, Lucia, alive.

title: US loses measles elimination status – an epidemiologist explains what it will take to regain it
paragraphs: The United States has lost its measles elimination status – an international designation reflecting an absence of local measles transmission for at least 12 months – a public health achievement held since 2000. A commission of the Pan American Health Organization, a regional office of the World Health Organization that oversees the Americas, reached that conclusion in November 2026, with a formal announcement expected Nov. 17.
Canada lost its measles elimination status in 2025, as did the United Kingdom and other countries in Europe and central Asia in early 2026.

These losses of status are no mystery. Measles is one of the most contagious diseases and still circulates in much of the world. What keeps the disease in check is herd immunity – when a high enough percentage of the population is vaccinated to break the chains of transmission. For measles, that’s at least 95%. But in 2025-26, only 92% of kindergartners in the U.S. received the measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine.

I’m an epidemiologist who studies misinformation in the same way others study smoking or air pollution: as an exposure that makes populations sick. For years I’ve watched vaccine misinformation help erode the coverage that kept measles from spreading.

A measles vaccine has existed in the U.S. since 1963. The combined MMR vaccine followed in 1971; two doses are about 97% effective. A federal program created in 1993 made it free for eligible children. After widespread vaccination efforts, reported cases dropped more than 99%, and by 2000 measles was declared eliminated.

But due to the success of the MMR vaccine, within a generation most parents and many doctors had never even seen a measles case. The experts who certified elimination in 2000 warned that maintaining elimination status would require sustained high rates of vaccination, fast outbreak response and strong surveillance. Drop any one of these conditions and imported cases would spread.
So how does a country with a 97% effective vaccine lose measles elimination status? One obvious explanation: The vaccine worked so well that people forgot what the disease does.

Before the vaccine, measles infected 3 million to 4 million Americans a year. Tens of thousands were hospitalized, and hundreds died. Parents didn’t need convincing. They had seen it. Even with most cases unreported, the official count in 1963 was nearly 400,000 cases.

About 1 in 20 children who contract measles develop pneumonia. The virus can also erase part of the immune system’s memory, an effect called immune amnesia, leaving children open to infections they had already beaten.
In rare cases, it causes a fatal brain disease, subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, which appears years after apparent recovery. In 2025, a child in Los Angeles died of it.

As of Nov. 12, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention counted 5,412 cases for 2026 – the highest number since 1991 – and 591 hospitalizations. Among children under 5, 1 in 6 have been hospitalized.

Six deaths appear in the CDC’s 2026 count, which now relies on federal death certificate data. States, using a broader definition, report a total of 10 deaths: seven in Pennsylvania, one in New York and two in Wisconsin.

Pennsylvania’s outbreak alone has produced 1,542 cases and 305 hospitalizations, by the state’s Nov. 13 count. Major outbreaks have also hit South Carolina, Utah and Arizona since the West Texas outbreak of early 2025, which was the start of the national surge of measles outbreaks. Utah’s outbreak, which began in June 2025, has gone well past the 12-month mark. That outbreak alone breaches the WHO’s definition of measles elimination and could have triggered the loss of elimination status.
When no one remembers the disease, the vaccine becomes the only thing left to fear. Misinformation feeds on that imbalance.

Parents who had never seen measles had nothing vivid to weigh against claims of vaccine risk, so even discredited risks felt plausible. A 1998 paper fraudulently linking MMR to autism was retracted in 2010, and its author lost his medical license. But the damage was already done, and this myth persists to this day, even though studies that included millions of children have found no link.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, vaccine misinformation proliferated in echo chambers on social media. It is no surprise that the percentage of kindergartners who have received their MMR shots has fallen every year since the 2019-20 school year.

In a 2025 KFF poll, parents who believed any false measles claim were more than twice as likely to have skipped or delayed vaccines. Since the COVID-19 pandemic, the anti-vaccine movement has also used the banner of medical freedom to gain a larger, more mainstream audience.
Now these arguments have found an audience in federal policy.

On Aug. 10, 2026, President Donald Trump signed an order calling for MMR to be split into three single-disease shots, which are not sold in the United States. There is no published evidence that separating MMR offers any benefit, and more doctor visits mean more chances for missed doses.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. suggested in August that Pennsylvania’s first two measles-associated deaths “may even have been altogether fabricated.” State officials had investigated both. While questioning the vaccine and measles deaths, he has promoted vitamin A and nutrition as measles cures. The CDC classifies vitamin A as a supportive treatment, not a cure or vaccine substitute.
Vaccination rates for the MMR vaccine among U.S. kindergartners fell from 95.2% in 2019-20 to 92.4% in 2025-26. Exemptions from any required vaccine rose to a record 4.2%.

Of this year’s cases, 96% were unvaccinated or of unknown status. The 92.4% kindergarten vaccination rate leaves about 280,000 kindergartners without documented MMR. Among states, Idaho has the lowest MMR rate with 75.2% among Idaho kindergartners, while some counties and communities there and elsewhere have even lower rates.
Adult immunity also has gaps: Adults are 41% of this year’s cases, and 15% of them were hospitalized. Many who were vaccinated before 1989, when a second MMR dose was added, got only one.

Regaining elimination status means the U.S experiencing at least 12 months without continuous transmission. That will require the same factors that led to the U.S. earning that status in 2000: stronger surveillance, speedy outbreak response and increased vaccination rates.

title: New England’s first Bible, published in an Indigenous language, had one aim: Converting Native Americans
paragraphs: In 1663, colonial printers in New England produced a translation of the Bible into Wampanoag, an Algonquian language spoken in southern New England. Also known as Wôpanâak or Massachusett, it was one of several Native American languages in the region.
Printing the book would be an important story on its own. But it is even more remarkable because it was the first Bible that English colonists published in North America.

As a historian of early America, I believe this Bible sheds important light on relations between New England’s Native peoples and English immigrants, who saw themselves as crucial players in the spread of Protestant Christianity. Consumed with the idea that their culture was superior, many English Protestants believed they could conquer North America without much bloodshed: that Indigenous peoples would voluntarily abandon their cultures and embrace the faith of the newcomers.

The historical record is more complex. My 2026 book, “Contested Continent,” details the struggle to control North America in the generations after Christopher Columbus crossed the Atlantic Ocean. There were many moments, including the fabled first Thanksgiving of 1621, when Indigenous peoples and colonists coexisted. But there was brutal violence as well, such as English colonists’ efforts to destroy the Pequot of southern New England in 1637.
In the aftermath of early warfare, some Puritan clerics looked for new ways to convert Native Americans – and decided religious texts were the answer.

During the Protestant Reformation, Martin Luther argued that the only infallible source of religious understanding was the Bible, a doctrine known as “sola scriptura.” Protestants believed the laity needed to become literate, in order to read Scripture for themselves.

The Puritans embraced this teaching, and in 1638, the Rev. Joseph Glover paid to transport a printing press to Cambridge, Massachusetts. Two years later, that press published the Bay Psalm Book, a collection of songs for worship – the first book printed in English North America.

In the years that followed, printers offered many religious tracts, often based on sermons. They believed that print would bring Protestant Christianity to a widening audience and provide guidance for existing believers.

A Puritan minister named John Eliot sailed from England to Boston in 1631 and soon took a leading role in the church at Roxbury, just south of the city. Eliot was so devoted to books that he purportedly brought 23 barrels of them with him from England.

By the 1640s, he began trying to spread his faith among Native residents of the region. To do so, he needed to be able to communicate with those he hoped to convert, and he understood that books could advance his cause.

Other colonists also hoped that print could foster good relations with the Native residents of New England. The most famous was Roger Williams, founder of Rhode Island. “A Key into the Language of America,” a book he published in London in 1643, provided phrases in Narragsansett, another Algonquian language. Such efforts were crucial to Europeans eager to trade with Native peoples – and to those, like Williams, who wanted to spread their culture without violence.

Eliot was intent on translating the Bible. He did not know Wampanoag, but he met an interpreter who impressed him: Cockenoe, a Montauk man from Long Island who had been taken captive during the Anglo-Pequot War in 1637. He became crucial to the Cambridge-educated cleric’s cause.

Eliot was unstinting in his praise of Cockenoe, whom he called a “pregnant witted young man.” He pronounced words clearly, which was crucial for Eliot: Like almost all Native languages in North America at the time, Wanpanoak did not have a writing system, so Eliot needed to transcribe what he heard.

Cockenoe’s instruction enabled Eliot to produce religious works in Wampanoag, including the Ten Commandments and the Lord’s Prayer. In 1663, printers Samuel Green and Marmaduke Johnson published “Mamusse Wunneetupanatamwe Up-Biblum God,” Eliot and Cockenoe’s full translation of the Bible.

Their Bible included some lines in English so that a literate person could recite the Native words out loud to others, even if they did not know the meaning. Green ordered enough paper to produce 1,000 copies of the book, although it is difficult to know how many existed.

Cockenoe was not the only Indigenous resident who worked on the Bible. Wawaus, a Nipmuc man from what is now central Massachusetts, helped set type for the book. Also known as James Printer, he was studying at Harvard’s Indian College, which had been established in 1655 to spread Christianity among Native peoples.
Eliot’s efforts to convert Indigenous peoples extended beyond translation, giving him the sobriquet “apostle to the Indians.”

He also worked with a missionary society to establish new towns where Algonquian-speaking peoples would abandon their traditional practices and live like colonists. Residents were to halt seasonal migrations, which had been crucial to their economies, and instead live year-round in houses. They were to dress like colonists, follow colonial laws and embrace Protestant religious practices.

Meanwhile, the growth of the colonial population was putting added pressure on Indigenous peoples who lived nearby. By the mid-1670s, any remaining goodwill between many Indigenous peoples and English colonists faded in a contest over limited resources, which was particularly difficult for Native Americans not living in the missionary communities.

In 1675, tensions erupted into what was called Metacom’s or King Philip’s War, named after the Wampanoag leader who led a widespread rebellion against colonists. The two-year conflict spread across southern New England and reached the shores of Casco Bay in present-day Maine. According to historian Jill Lepore, it was the deadliest war in American history, in proportion to the population.

Among the victims were the Native converts in the towns Eliot helped to establish, including Natick, a community west of Boston. Colonial authorities rounded them up, transported them to an island in Boston harbor and sold many into slavery. Even those who escaped the ravages of war found themselves struggling to maintain their shrinking lands.
Eliot believed that literacy was crucial for spreading his faith. In Cockenoe he found a talented partner. But mastering literacy could be a double-edged sword.

In 1676, in the midst of Metacom’s War, soldiers came across a note in English in the smoldering ruins of Medfield, a colonial town destroyed by Native Americans. Possibly written by Wawaus, the brief message warned that Indigenous residents would fight for years to maintain their lands.

Some colonizers, including Eliot, hoped to avoid using guns and bloodshed to advance their faith. But their goal was still destruction: to eliminate Algonquian cultures. As Wawaus’ note and Algonquian-speaking peoples’ presence in New England today reveal, those efforts failed.

title: MAHA suffered heavy losses in the 2026 midterms, but the movement is far from dead
paragraphs: Candidates tied to the Make America Healthy Again, or MAHA, movement suffered a series of electoral defeats in the 2026 midterm elections, raising questions about MAHA’s political future.

Despite its name, MAHA has become a controversial force in American health politics. While the movement calls for healthier food, increased physical activity and greater corporate transparency, prominent figures within it have also challenged established scientific evidence, especially on vaccines.

Some commentators and critics have described the defeat of MAHA-aligned candidates like Iowa gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn as a “brutal election night wipeout.” Others have asked whether MAHA is “dying.”

Yet many Americans still support MAHA and the policies it champions. Its supporters also continue to hold powerful positions in the Trump administration – like Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., National Institutes of Health Director Jay Bhattacharya, and Kyle Diamantas, acting commissioner of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration – even as a new Congress prepares to take office in January 2027.

We are political scientists who study public opinion on healthcare policy. We see MAHA’s electoral losses as a political setback, not a death sentence. The movement’s influence extends beyond its candidates and the elections they contest.
MAHA’s electoral losses came amid a potentially generational swing toward Democrats across the country,

More than half the 24 gubernatorial and Congressional candidates endorsed by MAHA’s political action committee, MAHA Action, lost their election bids. These included Lahn, Texas Senate candidate Ken Paxton and House candidate Vic Mellor in Rhode Island. Others, like incumbent Representative Anna Paulina Luna, R-FL, won by less than 1% in a district that she won by nearly 10 percentage points in 2024.

Lahn’s defeat stands out as a major loss. Lahn, a farmer who railed against pesticides on the campaign trail and promised to ban COVID-19 vaccinations in Iowa, was endorsed by Kennedy. Lahn has been described by some as a model MAHA candidate and received over US$1 million in campaign contributions from MAHA Action.

But the movement’s poor showing at the ballot box does not mean that some of MAHA’s ideas are unpopular among Americans. A May 2026 poll conducted by the health policy organization KFF found that 41% of American adults supported MAHA, including many Democrats and independents.

Many Americans also share MAHA’s concerns about food safety. According to KFF, 75% of Americans believe the government does too little to regulate chemical additives in food, while 64% say the same about agricultural pesticides.

Yet the popularity of MAHA policies did little to help MAHA-backed candidates win in the first election cycle where MAHA-aligned candidates were on the ballot. Following the midterm elections, some MAHA activists moved to blame President Donald Trump for failing to fulfill promises on these issues.

One prime example: In a postelection episode of Joe Rogan’s podcast, Calley Means, a former senior adviser to Kennedy, accused senior White House officials of allowing corporate interests to undermine MAHA’s goals. Dissatisfaction also spilled over to MAHA supporters in the general public, with one postelection poll finding that just over half of MAHA supporters feel the Trump administration made Americans’ health and well-being better throughout his second term in office.

Dissatisfaction with Trump, however, tells only part of the story. Another KFF poll conducted just before the election found that 42% of MAHA-supporting voters considered lowering healthcare costs their top health priority. By comparison, 21% prioritized restricting food additives, and 10% chose vaccine safety. Among voters more broadly, 55% believed Trump’s policies increased their healthcare costs, and 83% of those voters reported voting for Democrats. Most MAHA supporters, however, continued to vote for Republicans.

Supporting a movement, embracing its policy priorities and casting a ballot for its candidates do not necessarily go hand in hand. Americans can support MAHA’s goals without identifying with the movement or voting for its candidates. Likewise, MAHA supporters may vote Republican even when they are dissatisfied with Trump’s health policies. MAHA’s electoral losses, therefore, tell us little about how much support its ideas enjoy.

Despite its electoral losses, MAHA still holds considerable influence in Washington. Kennedy still leads HHS, where he can continue reshaping how the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention steers vaccine recommendations in a direction that aligns with his vaccine-skeptical views. These efforts face growing scrutiny amid public confusion over Kennedy’s vaccine guidance and reports that he sought to remove measles-related deaths from CDC statistics.

Kennedy appears undeterred by MAHA’s electoral setbacks. Following the election, he praised incoming White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, declaring, “Next to me, Stephen Miller is the strongest MAHA supporter in the administration. It’s time to unleash the Kraken.”

MAHA’s continued influence in the Trump administration, however, will face new obstacles now that Democrats control Congress. Facing greater opposition, the administration may increasingly rely on executive actions, including executive orders, new federal regulations and agency reports, to advance its health policies. However, Congress can also investigate HHS decisions and use its control over federal spending to limit what the agency can do.

MAHA’s political future remains uncertain. Some supporters may gradually move toward Democrats, particularly those concerned about corporate influence, pharmaceutical industry accountability and food safety. These concerns cross partisan lines, giving Democrats an opportunity to appeal to voters dissatisfied with Trump but still supportive of MAHA’s priorities.

MAHA could also become a movement independent of Trump and MAGA. It could bring together Americans who care about health and wellness, distrust major institutions and oppose corporate influence over food and medicine. Kennedy’s independent presidential campaign attracted as much as 15% support among voters in July 2024. This showed that an alternative to the two major parties could attract substantial support.

Whether MAHA remains tied to Trump’s increasingly divided coalition will shape its future beyond his presidency. The frustrations and health concerns that fueled its rise among Americans have not disappeared.

The authors do not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and have disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

title: Debate in New York City over city-run groceries is not just about food, but something bigger
paragraphs: New York City is moving closer to launching its effort to counter food inflation by opening five city-run grocery stores. Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced in May 2026 that the first store would open in the Hunts Point neighborhood of the South Bronx in 2027, with another in East Harlem to follow.

Five stores, one in each borough, are unlikely to substantially change grocery prices in a city with nearly 1,000 supermarkets and more than 8 million inhabitants. But each could make a meaningful difference to the grocery bills of local shoppers by selling essentials at below-market prices.

Even with just five planned stores set to open in lower-income neighborhoods, the initiative has ignited fierce opposition from independent grocers, supermarket trade associations and a coalition representing immigrant-owned food businesses.
What explains this pushback?

As a food policy scholar, I believe this opposition is about more than the immediate economic impact of five stores. It is about the precedent they could establish. Mamdani’s initiative challenges an entrenched expectation that the government should leave the provision of consumer goods to private enterprise even as it encourages businesses to invest in certain locations, regulates their activities and helps low-income shoppers through various food assistance programs.

The reality is more complicated. For at least a century, New York’s food economy has not operated independently of government. In fact, public policies and investments have long shaped where supermarkets open, which businesses can operate with a profit, and how residents obtain food.
It’s just that they have done so in ways consumers often don’t see.

That is why the five grocery stores carry a broader significance, in my view. They offer a different model of public investment that makes the government much more visible in providing an essential service – and more accountable for its results. New Yorkers will get an opportunity to judge that contribution directly.
If the stores succeed, they may change not just what people expect to pay for groceries, but what they expect their city government to provide.
New York City has committed US$70 million to develop these stores, which will be open to all.
While they will be managed by private operators, the city will provide rent-free space, prioritize publicly owned sites and ensure that essential foods are priced 30% below typical retail prices.
In this respect, the stores offer a “public option” – a government-provided good or service that exists alongside private alternatives, like public schools and city hospitals.

Municipal grocery stores would offer New Yorkers a similar choice alongside private retailers. But as a public option, they would create a visible alternative against which shoppers can judge privately owned stores, setting a benchmark for food prices and service quality. They would also demonstrate how public investment can be used to make an essential good more affordable.
At his May announcement, Mamdani described the proposed Bronx store and its surrounding development as “physical proof of our conviction that government can be a force for good.”
Government-supported food retailing has a long history in New York City despite opposition by existing businesses.

In 1934, Mayor Fiorello La Guardia’s administration began selling discounted milk to low-income families, but the initiative drew complaints from grocers about unfair competition. Independent merchants similarly protested the city’s efforts to subsidize a new Pathmark supermarket in East Harlem in the 1990s, warning that it would put local grocers out of business.

A more recent example is the city’s Food Retail Expansion to Support Health program, known as FRESH. Since 2009, it has offered supermarket developers and operators long-term tax breaks and zoning incentives to build or expand dozens of stores in underserved neighborhoods.
These incentives have helped increase grocery retail space, but shoppers don’t see the public support behind them.

FRESH is just one example of an approach toward supermarket financing that gained momentum in the 1990s, when governments sought to address social problems by encouraging private investment. Food insecurity was blamed on a scarcity of neighborhood supermarkets, not on prices being beyond reach for local shoppers.

Subsidizing new stores promised better nutrition and economic development without confronting poverty or inequality, and FRESH reflects that approach. Participating supermarkets must devote space to perishable foods, but they’re not required to offer affordable prices. That may be one reason why researchers have found that adding supermarkets to low-income neighborhoods, by itself, doesn’t substantially improve residents’ diets.

This hidden government role is hardly confined to grocery stores. Much of what government does for Americans is delivered indirectly, through tax credits, subsidies and private institutions. Because the public contribution is obscured, people often give credit to private markets for the benefits provided by public policy, from student loans to healthcare.
This invisibility is a consequence of policy design and influences how citizens understand government, a phenomenon that political scientist Suzanne Mettler described as “the submerged state.”
Municipal grocery stores depart from the traditional model in two important ways.

First, they make affordability an explicit condition of public investment rather than the outcome of increased retail competition. Second, they make government’s contribution visible. For example, the stores will share distinct branding so shoppers know who’s responsible for the affordable food.

title: National ground stop response highlights critical errors in public reassurance – saying ‘nothing nefarious’ did the opposite of quelling public concern
paragraphs: Thousands of travelers were stranded on Nov. 13, 2026, when the Federal Aviation Administration grounded all domestic flights in the U.S. because of what they said were failures in decades-old air traffic communications systems. Crisis communications expert Shannon A. Bowen, a scholar at the University of South Carolina’s College of Information and Communications, spoke with The Conversation’s Politics and Legal Affairs Editor, Naomi Schalit, about how the Trump administration handled the first day of the crisis.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
Is there a first principle in crisis communications?

The first principle would be to react quickly and react with accuracy, react with everything you know at the moment, truthfully, but always react quickly. Because if you delay until you gather information, a vacuum will ensue. Information fills that vacuum that may not be accurate. And so that’s the enemy of accurate crisis communication, but you want to always speak quickly and be the most authoritative and definitive source, even if very little information is known.
What did we see on the day of the ground stop?

A crisis unfolded and to the administration’s credit, they did react very quickly, in a way that offered the information that was known at the time, even though not a lot was known about why the ground stop was issued until later.
You’re speaking about the short press conference that afternoon with Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin?

He did keep saying that nothing nefarious was at hand. And for a crisis communication scholar, you would not want to introduce the idea that something nefarious was at hand, unless, indeed, something nefarious was at hand. So by the very act of introducing this concept and this idea, I think the talking point, “Nothing nefarious,” then went across multiple networks, and it became the center of a controversy rather than quelling a controversy.

By saying nothing nefarious is at hand, that indeed confirmed something nefarious was at hand, even if the nefariousness was only the mismanagement of the air traffic control systems routers that they claimed caused the problem. By introducing this idea, I believe it did bring to mind that there may be other state actors behind whatever happened, that it could be a cyber attack. It would have been better to say, “We have evidence that this was not a cyber attack but a hardware failure.”
How did the later press conference with Mullin and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy go from your perspective as an expert on crisis communications?
They handled the questions that they received correctly. They told us as much information as they knew.
However, they did seem to downplay the extent of this crisis, because we have to remember the traveling public is not just people trying to get to business meetings.

We had football teams stranded. Now football Saturday, all over the SEC, has been disrupted. And there’s probably disruption in other areas of the country, but to us in the South, SEC football is almost a religious experience on Saturday. Luckily, the University of South Carolina football team had already flown out. But our marching band was stuck in this crisis, and so we have a lot of ripple effects from something like this happening, and it definitely says to me that this was an emergency situation. It wasn’t simply a crisis, it was an actual emergency of impending disaster-level scale.

If it were simply routers being overloaded, as we’ve been told, why wouldn’t they already know this situation and restart those routers the night before or over Friday night after most of the traveling public is out of the air?
What was Mullin’s and Duffy’s job when they got out there? What did they need to do?

To inform the public about the danger, why this happened, the extent of the problem, and what they’re doing to remediate the problem. We keep hearing that they’re asking for US$30 billion and more to repair the whole infrastructure for the air traffic control system, which is great, but what are they doing right now?

How do we know that flights in the air, right this minute, are any safer than the ones yesterday, a minute before the ground stop? Do we have that information? I don’t feel confident that they addressed that question appropriately. I don’t think that the traveling public entirely feels safe at this point or adequately informed that they will arrive at their destination.
They introduced politics into the press conference as well, didn’t they?

It’s something that they have the prerogative to do. They are both political appointees and members of the cabinet. So I understand that aspect, but I really wish they had addressed the traveling public’s concerns more overtly before making it political, that they need more money to fix this. We know they need more money to fix it, and I’m sure the American taxpayers are aware of the problem and willing to fund those corrections. But the more expedient issues would be, what about all these people who were stuck in airports?
Were there warning signs for this crisis?

I believe there were. We had another ground stop about three years ago, due to air traffic control problems, and that is what we call in crisis communications a “prodrome,” a warning sign of larger impending problems. When you see these types of warning signs, it really gives us a reason to think it’s going to get worse.

Duffy did say on Nov. 13 that, because of the condition of the air traffic infrastructure, “you will have more” ground stoppages. If you had a piece of advice for the administration regarding their future communications, what would you tell them?

I would say to communicate in advance as much as possible, so if you’re even considering a ground stop, it may be a good idea to put out a public notice so that people don’t go to the airport on a vacation flight, maybe they delay that for a week or two. It might also be a good idea to speak with the airline industry representatives and say, “Here’s what we’re thinking. Can you work with us? How can we make this better for the traveling public?” Also, if 17 of 22 routers were malfunctioning, could we have had a partial ground stop at only the affected airports, rather than a nationwide stop?
My silly last question: Do crisis communications experts have any theories about Friday the 13th?

title: To get Americans to care about climate change, just call it climate change
paragraphs: You may be hearing phrases like “climate crisis,” “climate emergency” and “climate justice” a lot as the 2026 United Nations climate summit is underway. Political leaders, including U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres, are using them to try to get across the urgent risks and consequences of climate change. The danger is real, but is using this language actually persuasive?

It turns out that Americans are more familiar with – and more concerned about – climate change and global warming than they are about climate crisis, climate emergency or climate justice, according to a survey we conducted with a nationally representative sample of 5,137 Americans.
Moreover, we found no evidence that the alternative terms increased people’s sense of urgency, willingness to support climate-friendly policies or willingness to act.

The familiar terms – climate change and global warming – did at least as well, and sometimes better, than climate crisis and climate emergency in eliciting concern, perceived urgency and willingness to act. The phrase climate justice consistently tended to do worse, likely in part because it was the least familiar. These response patterns were similar among Republicans, Democrats and independents.
In our work as research psychologists, we have explored how Americans respond to the ways climate change is communicated and have uncovered a need to use straightforward language.

For example, people we interviewed for a study published in 2021 felt that climate experts were talking over their heads with terms like “adaptation,” “mitigation,” “sustainability” and “carbon-dioxide removal.” They wanted experts to use more familiar terms instead.

This inspired us to write a quick guide to climate jargon, published in The Conversation. Using everyday language makes information easier to understand, and even highly educated people tend to prefer it.

Jargon like “biodiversity loss” has similar problems. That refers to the shrinking variety of life on Earth, which is exacerbated by climate change. A survey of 7,338 U.S. adults led by one of us found people were much more familiar with and more concerned about “extinction of plants and animals” – or, if an explanation was provided, “nature loss”.

Even with an explanation, “biodiversity loss” was the least familiar and of least concern for people among several terms. Most people didn’t find “biodiversity crisis” or “extinction crisis” familiar either.
Yet, experts often use complex jargon because it is familiar to them, and they may not realize it is unfamiliar to others.

It has become common to talk about climate change and global warming as if they have the same meaning, but there are differences. Climate change refers to changes in the overall climate, while global warming refers specifically to rising temperatures.

A historical review found that, in the past, people were less likely to associate the term climate change with the idea that humans are actively warming the planet than they were with the term global warming. Perhaps this is why Democrats used to like the term global warming, while the popularization of the term climate change has been credited to Frank Luntz, an adviser to the George W. Bush administration.

Past surveys also found that Democrats used to think of global warming as being more serious than climate change, while Republicans thought of climate change as more serious than global warming. But according to a recent review, these partisan differences have now faded.

Alternative terms such as climate crisis, climate emergency and climate justice have been used to emphasize other aspects of climate change and to try to raise concern. In 2019, the British newspaper The Guardian switched to using climate crisis and climate emergency because it wanted to convey urgency.

Activists use the term climate justice to draw attention to climate change as a human rights challenge: Low-income people around the world suffer the most from the effects of climate change, despite being the least responsible for causing it.
Right now, the terms climate crisis, climate emergency or climate justice are less familiar and elicit less concern than climate change or global warming.

Even if these terms become more commonplace, there is no guarantee that they will heighten concern or inspire action. In fact, studies have suggested that phrases like climate crisis could backfire if they don’t resonate with people.

Our advice: Don’t make the mistake of using overheated language. Just stick with familiar terms that people understand – use global warming when referring to rising temperatures and climate change for overall changes in the climate.
